steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an import statement that brings React and useState into your file.
successCriteria: The code must include a valid import statement that imports both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but your import statement isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look like a valid import statement for React and useState. Remember to use the correct syntax: import React, { useState } from 'react';

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. The component should be defined with TypeScript syntax.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function. Make sure to include a return statement with some JSX content.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a functional App component that returns JSX.
successCriteria: Component named App is defined
Component returns JSX
Component uses TypeScript syntax
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your component is named 'App', returns JSX, and uses TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't quite right. Check that you've defined a component named 'App' that returns JSX with TypeScript syntax.

steps.title: Define a User interface
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface named User with id (number), name (string), email (string), and active (boolean) properties. Define this interface above your App component.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: A User interface is defined with the correct properties and types, ready to be used in the component.
successCriteria: The code includes an interface named User with id: number, name: string, email: string, and active: boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the User interface with all required properties and proper TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your User interface has all four properties (id, name, email, active) with the correct TypeScript types (number, string, string, boolean).
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword, name it 'User', and include id (number), name (string), email (string), and active (boolean) properties.

steps.title: Initialize user state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, initialize a state variable called 'user' using useState. The state should have the type User (the interface you defined earlier) and be initialized with an empty object that matches the User interface structure.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a generic type parameter <User> to specify the state type. Provide an initial value that matches all required properties of the User interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component should now have a typed state variable 'user' initialized with default values that match the User interface.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called inside the App component
The state variable is named 'user'
The useState call includes the generic type <User>
An initial value object is provided with all required User properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized typed state using useState with the User interface. This ensures type safety for the user state throughout your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've included all required elements: 1) useState hook inside the component, 2) state variable named 'user', 3) generic type <User>, and 4) an initial object with all User interface properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization is missing key elements. Remember to use useState with the User type and provide an initial object that matches the User interface structure.

steps.title: Create a Partial<User> update object
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a variable named 'partialUpdate' of type 'Partial<User>' with some properties from the User interface (e.g., name and isActive).
steps.hint: Use the Partial utility type to define an object that may contain only some properties of User. Initialize it with at least one property.
steps.expectedOutcome: A variable 'partialUpdate' of type Partial<User> is created inside the component, demonstrating how Partial utility type allows partial updates.
successCriteria: The code should include a variable named 'partialUpdate' with type annotation 'Partial<User>' and at least one property from the User interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a Partial<User> variable. This shows how Partial utility type allows you to create objects with only some properties of the original type.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a variable named 'partialUpdate' with the type 'Partial<User>' and included at least one property from the User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a variable named 'partialUpdate' with type 'Partial<User>' inside the App component, and initialize it with at least one property from the User interface.

steps.title: Create a Readonly<User> object
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a variable named 'readonlyUser' with the type Readonly<User> and assign it an object that matches the User interface structure.
steps.hint: Use the Readonly utility type to wrap your User interface. This will make all properties of the object immutable.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a readonlyUser variable that demonstrates how the Readonly utility type prevents modifications to object properties.
successCriteria: Variable named 'readonlyUser'
Type annotation uses 'Readonly<User>'
Object contains all required User properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a Readonly<User> object. This utility type makes all properties of the object immutable, preventing accidental modifications.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've created a variable named 'readonlyUser' with the type Readonly<User> and assigned it a complete User object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to create a variable named 'readonlyUser' with the type Readonly<User> and assign it an object with all the required User properties.

steps.title: Create a Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> object
steps.instruction: Create a variable named 'contactInfo' with the type Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and assign it an object containing only the 'name' and 'email' properties from the user state.
steps.hint: Use the Pick utility type to select specific properties from the User interface. The syntax is Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a variable 'contactInfo' that uses the Pick utility type to select only the 'name' and 'email' properties from the User interface.
successCriteria: Variable named 'contactInfo'
Type annotation uses Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>
Object contains 'name' and 'email' properties
Values match user state properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully used the Pick utility type to create an object with only selected properties from the User interface.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the exact type Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and including both 'name' and 'email' properties in the object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The variable 'contactInfo' should use the Pick utility type with the User interface, selecting only 'name' and 'email' properties.

steps.title: Create an Omit<User, 'id' | 'active'> object
steps.instruction: Create a variable named 'userWithoutId' with the type Omit<User, 'id' | 'active'> and assign it an object containing only the 'name' and 'email' properties from the user object.
steps.hint: Use the Omit utility type to create a type that excludes the 'id' and 'active' properties from the User interface. Then create an object with the remaining properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a variable 'userWithoutId' of type Omit<User, 'id' | 'active'> that contains an object with name and email properties.
successCriteria: The variable must be named 'userWithoutId', use the Omit utility type with User interface and exclude 'id' and 'active', and contain an object with name and email properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully used the Omit utility type to create a type that excludes specific properties from the User interface.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're using the correct property names to exclude ('id' and 'active') and that your object contains only 'name' and 'email' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Omit utility type wasn't implemented correctly. Remember to exclude 'id' and 'active' from the User type and create an object with the remaining properties.

steps.title: Add a container div to the component return
steps.instruction: Wrap the existing content in the App component's return statement with a div element that has the className 'app-container'.
steps.hint: Add a div with className='app-container' around the existing h1 element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component's return statement should have a div with className 'app-container' wrapping the h1 element.
successCriteria: The code must include a div element with className='app-container' that wraps the existing h1 element in the return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a container div with the correct className. This provides a structural wrapper for the utility type examples we'll display.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've wrapped the h1 element with a div that has className='app-container'. Check that the className attribute is properly set.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container div with className 'app-container' is missing or incorrect. Look at the return statement and ensure you've wrapped the h1 element with a div that has the correct className attribute.

steps.title: Display the original User state
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement, add a section to display the current 'user' state values. Create a <div> with a heading 'Original User' and display each property (id, name, email, isActive) in separate paragraphs.
steps.hint: You can access the user object properties directly (e.g., user.name). Add this section after the existing <h1> element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the original user object values (id: 1, name: 'John Doe', email: 'john@example.com', isActive: true) in a structured format.

steps.title: Add update button with Partial<User> handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside the return statement that, when clicked, updates the user state using the existing userUpdate object. The button should have an onClick handler that calls setUser with a new object that merges the current user with userUpdate.
steps.hint: Use the setUser function from useState to update the state. Since userUpdate is a Partial<User>, you can spread both objects to create a complete User object.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a button that updates state with a partial object
<button onClick={() => setState(prev => ({ ...prev, ...partialUpdate }))}>
  Update State
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button appears in the UI that, when clicked, updates the user state by merging the existing user with the userUpdate object, changing the name to 'Jane Doe' and isActive to false.
successCriteria: The button must be inside the return statement's JSX, have an onClick handler that calls setUser, and correctly merge userUpdate with the current user state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that uses the Partial<User> object to update state. This demonstrates how utility types like Partial can be used in real event handlers.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your onClick handler properly merges the userUpdate object with the current user state using the spread operator.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or its onClick handler isn't quite right. Remember to use setUser to update the state and merge the existing user with the userUpdate object.
